Main.sentence: Thomas Allen Coburn (March 14, 1948 – March 28, 2020) was an American politician and ___E:physician U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_doctor)___ who served as a ___E:United States senator U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_senator)___ from ___E:Oklahoma U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma)___ from 2005 to 2015. A ___E:Republican U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States))___ , Coburn previously served as a ___E:United States representative U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_representative)___ from 1995 to 2001.
Coburn was an obstetrician who operated a private medical practice in ___E:Muskogee, Oklahoma U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muskogee,_Oklahoma)___ .

He was elected to the ___E:United States House of Representatives U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives)___ in ___E:1994 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections)___ as part of the ___E:Republican Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Revolution)___ .

After being re-elected twice, Coburn upheld his ___E:campaign pledge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campaign_promise)___ to serve no more than three consecutive terms and did not seek re-election in ___E:2000 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections)___ .
In ___E:2004 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_United_States_Senate_election_in_Oklahoma)___ , he returned to political life with a successful run for the United States Senate.

Coburn was re-elected to a second Senate term in ___E:2010 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_United_States_Senate_election_in_Oklahoma)___ and kept his pledge not to seek a third term in 2016.  In January 2014, Coburn announced that he would resign before the expiration of his final term due to a recurrence of prostate cancer.

He submitted a letter of resignation to ___E:Oklahoma Governor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_Governor)___ ___E:Mary Fallin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Fallin)___ , effective at the end of the ___E:113th Congress U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/113th_Congress)___ .

Coburn was a ___E:fiscal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiscal_conservatism)___ and ___E:social conservative U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_conservatism)___ known for his opposition to ___E:deficit spending U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deficit_spending)___ , ___E:pork barrel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pork_barrel)___ projects,    and ___E:abortion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_in_the_United_States)___ .

Described as "the godfather of the modern conservative austerity movement",  he supported ___E:term limits U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Term_limit)___ , ___E:gun rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gun_politics_in_the_United_States)___ and the ___E:death penalty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment_in_the_United_States)___ ,  and opposed ___E:same-sex marriage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Same-sex_marriage_in_the_United_States)___ and ___E:embryonic stem cell research U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embryonic_stem_cell_research)___ .
Many Democrats referred to him as " ___E:Dr. No U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_No)___ " due to his frequent use of technicalities to block federal spending bills.

After leaving Congress, Coburn worked with the ___E:Manhattan Institute for Policy Research U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Institute_for_Policy_Research)___ on its efforts to reform the ___E:Food and Drug Administration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Drug_Administration)___ ,  becoming a senior fellow of the institute in December 2016.  Coburn also served as a senior advisor to ___E:Citizens for Self-Governance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizens_for_Self-Governance)___ , where he was active in calling for a ___E:convention to propose amendments to the United States Constitution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convention_to_propose_amendments_to_the_United_States_Constitution)___ .
Coburn was born in ___E:Casper, Wyoming U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casper,_Wyoming)___ , the son of Anita Joy (née Allen) and Orin Wesley Coburn.

Coburn's father was an ___E:optician U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optician)___ and founder of Coburn Optical Industries, and a named donor to ___E:O. W. Coburn School of Law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O._W._Coburn_School_of_Law)___ at ___E:Oral Roberts University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oral_Roberts_University)___ .

Coburn graduated with a ___E:Bachelor of Science U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science)___ in accounting from ___E:Oklahoma State University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_State_University)___ ,  where he was also a member of ___E:Sigma Nu U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigma_Nu)___ fraternity.

In 1968, he married Carolyn Denton,  the 1967 ___E:Miss Oklahoma U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_Oklahoma)___ ;  their three daughters are Callie,  Katie and ___E:Sarah U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Coburn)___ , a leading operatic ___E:soprano U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soprano)___ .
One of the top ten seniors in the School of Business, Coburn served as president of the College of Business Student Council.

From 1970 to 1978, Coburn served as a manufacturing manager at the Ophthalmic Division of Coburn Optical Industries in ___E:Colonial Heights, Virginia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonial_Heights,_Virginia)___ .
While Coburn was manager, the Virginia division of Coburn Optical grew from 13 employees to over 350 and captured 35 percent of the U.S. market.

After recovering from an occurrence of malignant ___E:melanoma U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melanoma)___ , Coburn pursued a medical degree and graduated from the ___E:University of Oklahoma Medical School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oklahoma_College_of_Medicine)___ with honors in 1983.  He then opened Maternal & Family Practice in Muskogee, Oklahoma, and served as a deacon in a ___E:Southern Baptist Church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Baptist_Convention)___ .

During his career in ___E:obstetrics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obstetrics)___ , he treated over 15,000 patients, delivered 4,000 babies and was subject to one ___E:malpractice U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malpractice)___ lawsuit, which was dismissed without finding Coburn at fault.
Together Coburn and his wife were members of First Baptist Church of Muskogee.

A ___E:sterilization U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_sterilization_(surgical_procedure))___ Coburn performed on a 20-year-old woman, Angela Plummer, in 1990, became what was called "the most incendiary issue" of his Senate campaign.

Coburn performed the sterilization on the woman during an emergency surgery to treat a life-threatening ___E:ectopic pregnancy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ectopic_pregnancy)___ , removing her healthy intact ___E:fallopian tube U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallopian_tube)___ as well as the one damaged by the surgery.
The woman sued Coburn, alleging that he did not have consent to sterilize her, while Coburn claimed he had her oral consent.
The lawsuit was ultimately dismissed with no finding of liability on Coburn's part.

The state attorney general claimed that Coburn committed ___E:Medicaid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicaid)___ ___E:fraud U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraud)___ by not reporting the sterilization when he filed a claim for the emergency surgery.

Medicaid did not reimburse doctors for sterilization procedures for patients under 21 and according to the attorney general, Coburn would not have been reimbursed at all had he disclosed this information.
Coburn says since he did not file a claim for the sterilization, no fraud was committed.
No charges were filed against Coburn for this claim.

In 1994, Coburn ran for the ___E:House of Representatives U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives)___ in ___E:Oklahoma's 2nd congressional district U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma%27s_2nd_congressional_district)___ , which was based in Muskogee and included 22 counties in northeastern Oklahoma.
Coburn initially expected to face eight-term incumbent ___E:Mike Synar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Synar)___ .
However, Synar was defeated in a runoff for the Democratic nomination by a 71-year-old retired ___E:principal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_(school))___ , Virgil Cooper.
According to Coburn's 2003 book, Breach of Trust: How Washington Turns Outsiders Into Insiders , Coburn and Cooper got along well, since both were opposed to the more liberal Synar.
The general election was cordial since both men knew that Synar would not return to Washington regardless of the outcome.
Coburn won by a 52%–48% margin, becoming the first Republican to represent the district since 1921.
Coburn was one of the most ___E:conservative U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservatism)___ members of the House.

He supported "reducing the size of the ___E:federal budget U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_budget_(United_States))___ ," wanted to make ___E:abortion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion)___ illegal and supported the proposed television ___E:V-chip U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V-chip)___ legislation.

Despite representing a heavily Democratic district and President ___E:Bill Clinton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton)___ 's electoral dominance therein, Coburn was reelected in 1996 and 1998.

In the House, Coburn earned a reputation as a political maverick due to his frequent battles with ___E:House Speaker U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_of_the_U.S._House_of_Representatives)___ ___E:Newt Gingrich U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newt_Gingrich)___ .

Most of these stand-offs stemmed from his belief that the Republican caucus was moving toward the ___E:political center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_center)___ and away from the more conservative ___E:Contract With America U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contract_With_America)___ policy proposals that had brought the Republicans into power in Congress in 1994 for the first time in 40 years.

Coburn endorsed conservative activist and former diplomat ___E:Alan Keyes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Keyes)___ in the ___E:2000 Republican presidential primaries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Republican_Party_presidential_primaries)___ .
Coburn retired from Congress in 2001, fulfilling his pledge to serve no more than three terms in the House.
His congressional district returned to the Democratic fold, as attorney ___E:Brad Carson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brad_Carson)___ defeated Andy Ewing, a Republican endorsed by Coburn.

After leaving the House and returning to private medical practice, Coburn wrote Breach of Trust , with ___E:ghostwriter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghostwriter)___ John Hart, about his experiences in Congress.
The book detailed Coburn's perspective on the internal Republican Party debates over the Contract With America and displayed his disdain for career politicians.

Some of the figures he criticized (such as Gingrich) were already out of office at the time of the book's publishing, but others (such as former House Speaker ___E:Dennis Hastert U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Hastert)___ ) remained influential in Congress, which resulted in speculation that some congressional Republicans wanted no part of Coburn's return to politics.
During his tenure in the House, Coburn wrote and passed far-reaching pieces of legislation.

These include laws to expand seniors' health care options, to protect access to home health care in rural areas and to allow Americans to access cheaper medications from ___E:Canada U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada)___ and other nations.
Coburn also wrote a law intended to prevent the spread of ___E:AIDS U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIDS)___ to infants.

The Wall Street Journal said about the law, "In 10 long years of AIDS politics and funding, this is actually the first legislation to pass in this country that will rescue babies." He also wrote a law to renew and reform federal AIDS care programs.

In 2002, President ___E:George W. Bush U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush)___ chose Coburn to serve as co-chair of the ___E:Presidential Advisory Council on HIV/AIDS U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Advisory_Council_on_HIV/AIDS)___ (PACHA).
During his three terms in the House, Coburn also played an influential role in reforming welfare and other federal entitlement programs.

As a congressman in 1997, Coburn protested ___E:NBC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC)___ 's plan to air the ___E:R-rated U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MPAA_film_rating_system)___ ___E:Academy Award U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards)___ -winning ___E:Holocaust U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocaust)___ drama Schindler's List during ___E:prime time U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_time)___ .

Coburn stated that, in airing the movie without editing it for television, TV had been taken "to an all-time low, with ___E:full-frontal nudity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full-frontal_nudity)___ , violence and profanity."   He also said the TV broadcast should outrage parents and decent-minded individuals everywhere.
Coburn described the airing of Schindler's List on television as "irresponsible sexual behavior.
I cringe when I realize that there were children all across this nation watching this program."
This statement met with strong criticism, as the film deals mainly with ___E:the Holocaust U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Holocaust)___ .

After heavy criticism, Coburn apologized "to all those I have offended" and clarified that he agreed with the movie being aired on television, but stated that it should have been on later in the evening.

In apologizing, Coburn said that at that time of the evening there are still large numbers of children watching without parental supervision and stated that he stood by his message of protecting children from violence, but had expressed it poorly.
He also said, "My intentions were good, but I've obviously made an error in judgment in how I've gone about saying what I wanted to say."

He later wrote in Breach of Trust that he considered this one of the biggest mistakes in his life and that, while he still felt the material was unsuitable for a 7 p.m. television broadcast, he handled the situation poorly.

After three years out of politics, Coburn announced his candidacy for the Senate seat being vacated by four-term incumbent ___E:Republican U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States))___ ___E:Don Nickles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Nickles)___ .

Former ___E:Oklahoma City U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_City)___ Mayor ___E:Kirk Humphreys U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Humphreys)___ (the favorite of the state and national Republican establishment) and Corporation Commissioner ___E:Bob Anthony U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Anthony)___ joined the field before Coburn.
However, Coburn won the primary by an unexpectedly large margin, taking 61% of the vote to Humphreys's 25%.

In the general election, he faced ___E:Brad Carson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brad_Carson)___ , the Democrat who had succeeded him in the 2nd District and was giving up his seat after only two terms.
In the election, Coburn won by a margin of 53% to Carson's 42%.

While Carson routed Coburn in the generally heavily Democratic 2nd District, Coburn swamped Carson in the ___E:Oklahoma City U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_City)___ metropolitan area and the closer-in ___E:Tulsa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulsa)___ suburbs.

Coburn won the state's two largest counties, Tulsa and ___E:Oklahoma U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_County)___ , by a combined 86,000 votes, more than half of his overall margin of 166,000 votes cast.
Coburn's Senate voting record was as conservative as his House record.
Coburn was re-elected in 2010. He received 90% of the vote in the Republican primary and 70% in the general election.

While he already planned on not seeking a third term in the Senate due to his self-imposed two-term term limit, on January 16, 2014, Coburn announced he would resign his office before his term ended at the end of the year due to his declining health.

On April 29, 2014, Coburn introduced the ___E:Insurance Capital Standards Clarification Act of 2014 (S. 2270; 113th Congress) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insurance_Capital_Standards_Clarification_Act_of_2014_(S._2270;_113th_Congress))___ into the Senate and it passed on June 3, 2014.
Coburn used the ___E:Senate hold U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_hold)___ privilege to prevent several bills from coming to the Senate floor.
Coburn earned a reputation for his use of this procedural mechanism.

In November 2009 Coburn drew attention for placing a hold on a ___E:veterans benefits U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veterans_benefits)___ bill known as the Veterans' Caregiver and Omnibus Health Benefits Act.   Coburn also placed a hold on a bill intended to help end hostilities in ___E:Uganda U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda)___ by the ___E:Lord's Resistance Army U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord%27s_Resistance_Army)___ .
On May 23, 2007, Coburn blocked two bills honoring the 100th birthday of ___E:Rachel Carson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Carson)___ .

Coburn called Carson's scientific work " ___E:junk science U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junk_science)___ ," proclaiming that Carson's landmark book Silent Spring was "the catalyst in the deadly worldwide stigmatization against ___E:insecticides U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insecticides)___ , especially ___E:DDT U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DDT)___ ."  Democratic Senator ___E:Benjamin L. Cardin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Cardin)___ of ___E:Maryland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland)___ had intended to submit a resolution celebrating Carson for her "legacy of scientific rigor coupled with poetic sensibility,"  but Coburn blocked it, saying that "the junk science and stigma surrounding DDT—the cheapest and most effective insecticide on the planet—have finally been jettisoned."

In response to Coburn's holds, ___E:Senate Majority Leader U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_leaders_of_the_United_States_Senate)___ ___E:Harry Reid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Reid)___ introduced the Advancing America's Priorities Act, ___E:S. 3297 U:(https://www.congress.gov/bill/110th-congress/senate-bill/3297)___ , in July 2008. S. 3297 combined thirty-five bills which Coburn had blocked into what Democrats called the "Tomnibus" bill.   The bill included health care provisions, new penalties for ___E:child pornography U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_pornography)___ , and several natural resources bills.
The bill failed a ___E:cloture U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloture)___ vote.

Coburn opposed parts of the legislation creating the Lewis and Clark ___E:Mount Hood U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Hood)___ Wilderness Area, which would add protections to wildlands in ___E:Oregon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon)___ , ___E:Washington U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state))___ , and ___E:Idaho U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idaho)___ .
Coburn exercised a hold on the legislation in both March and November 2008,   and decried the required $10 million for surveying and mapping as wasteful.
The Mount Hood bill would have been the largest amount of land added to federal protection since 1984.

In March 2009, those ___E:wilderness areas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilderness_areas)___ became protected under the ___E:Omnibus Public Land Management Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omnibus_Public_Land_Management_Act)___ , which passed the Senate 73–21.

According to the Boston Globe , Coburn initially blocked passage of the ___E:Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_Information_Nondiscrimination_Act)___ (GINA), objecting to provisions in the bill that allow discrimination based on genetic information from embryos and fetuses.
After the embryo loophole was closed, Coburn lifted his hold on the bill.
Coburn had initially blocked passage of the LRA Disarmament and Northern Uganda Recovery Act, which would help to disarm the Lord's Resistance Army, a political group accused of human rights abuses.

On March 9, 2010, Coburn lifted his hold on the LRA bill freeing it to move to the Senate floor after reaching a compromise regarding the funding of the bill,  and an eleven-day protest outside of his office.
Coburn was affiliated with a religious organization called ___E:The Family U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Family_(Christian_political_organization))___ .

Coburn previously lived in one of the Family's ___E:Washington, D.C. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C.)___ dormitories with then-Senator ___E:John Ensign U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Ensign)___ , another Family member and longtime resident of the ___E:C Street Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C_Street_Center)___ who admitted he had an extramarital affair with a staffer in 2009. The announcement by Ensign of his infidelity brought public scrutiny of the Family and its connection to other high-ranking politicians, including Coburn.

Coburn, together with senior members of the Family, attempted to intervene to end Ensign's affair in February 2008, before the affair became public, including by meeting with the husband of Ensign's mistress and encouraging Ensign to write a letter to his mistress breaking off the affair.

Ensign was driven to a branch of ___E:FedEx U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FedEx)___ from the C Street Center to post the letter, shortly after which Ensign called to tell his mistress to ignore it.

Coburn refused to speak about his involvement in Ensign's affair or his knowledge of the affair well before it became public, asserting legal privilege due to his statuses as a licensed physician in Oklahoma and a deacon.
In October 2009, Coburn made a statement to The New York Times about Ensign's affair and cover-up: "John got trapped doing something really stupid and then made a lot of other mistakes afterward.
Judgment gets impaired by arrogance and that's what's going on here."
In May 2011, the Senate Ethics Committee identified Coburn in their report on the ___E:ethics violations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Ensign_scandal)___ of Ensign.
The report stated that Coburn knew about Ensign's extramarital affair and was involved in trying to negotiate a financial settlement to cover it up.
Coburn was involved in the Bush Administration's struggle with Congress over ___E:whistleblower U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whistleblower)___ rights.

In the case of Garcetti v. Ceballos , the ___E:U.S. Supreme Court U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Supreme_Court)___ ruled that ___E:government employees U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_service)___ who testify against their employers did not have protection from retaliation by their employers under the ___E:First Amendment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution)___ of the Constitution.
The ___E:free speech U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_speech)___ protections of the First Amendment have long been used to shield whistleblowers from retaliation.

In response to the Supreme Court decision, the House passed H.R. 985, the Whistleblower Protection Act of 2007. Bush, citing ___E:national security U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_security)___ concerns, promised to ___E:veto U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veto)___ the bill should it be passed by Congress.

The Senate's version of the Whistleblower Protection Act (S. 274) was approved by the ___E:Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_Committee_on_Homeland_Security_and_Governmental_Affairs)___ on June 13, 2007. However, that version failed to reach a vote by the Senate, as Coburn placed a hold on the bill; effectively preventing the passage of the bill, which had bipartisan support in the Senate.
Coburn's website features a news item about ___E:United Nations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations)___ whistleblower Mathieu Credo Koumoin, a former employee for the U.N.

Development Program in West Africa, who has asked U.N. ethics chief ___E:Robert Benson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Benson_(United_Nations_ethics_chief)&action=edit&redlink=1)___ for protection under the U.N.'s whistleblower protection rules.

The site has a link to the "United Nations Watch" of the Republican Office of the ___E:Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Homeland_Security_and_Governmental_Affairs)___ ' Subcommittee on Federal Financial Management, Government Information and International Security, of which he was the ranking minority member.
Coburn's website also features a tip line for potential whistleblowers on government waste and fraud.

Coburn joined Congressmen ___E:Sue Myrick U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Myrick)___ (R- ___E:NC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina)___ ), ___E:Trent Franks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trent_Franks)___ (R- ___E:AZ U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona)___ ), ___E:John Shadegg U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Shadegg)___ (R-AZ), ___E:Paul Broun U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Broun)___ (R- ___E:GA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state))___ ) and ___E:Patrick McHenry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_McHenry)___ (R-NC) in a letter to ___E:IRS Commissioner U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IRS_Commissioner)___ ___E:Douglas H. Shulman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Shulman)___ on November 16, 2009, asking that the ___E:Council on American-Islamic Relations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_on_American-Islamic_Relations)___ (CAIR) be investigated for excessive lobbying and failing to register as a lobbying organization.

The request came in the wake of the publication of a book, Muslim Mafia , the foreword of which had been penned by Myrick, that portrayed CAIR as a subversive organization allied with international ___E:terrorists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrorism)___ .

On May 26, 2011, Coburn released a 73-page report, " ___E:National Science Foundation: Under the Microscope U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Science_Foundation:_Under_the_Microscope)___ ",   receiving attention from The New York Times , ___E:Fox News U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_News)___ and ___E:MSNBC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MSNBC)___ .
Coburn was one of three senators who voted against the ___E:Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STOCK_Act)___ (STOCK Act).
On February 3, 2012, Coburn released the following statement regarding the Act:
It's disappointing the Senate spent a week debating a bill that duplicates existing law and fails to address the real problems facing the country.

The only way we can restore confidence in Congress is to make hard choices and solve real problems by doing things like reforming our tax code, repairing our safety net and reducing our crushing debt burden.
Doing anything less will further alienate the American people and rightfully so.
Coburn was a member of the following committees:
Coburn opposed ___E:abortion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_in_the_United_States)___ , with the exception of abortions necessary to save the life of the mother.

In 2000, he sponsored a bill to prevent the ___E:Food and Drug Administration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Drug_Administration)___ from developing, testing, or approving the ___E:abortifacient U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortifacient)___ ___E:RU-486 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RU-486)___ .

On July 13, the bill failed in the House of Representatives by a vote of 182 to 187.  On the issue, Coburn sparked controversy with his remark, "I favor the death penalty for abortionists and other people who take life."   He noted that his great-grandmother was ___E:raped U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rape)___ by a sheriff.
